concept.name: Error-correction model
concept.definition: A dynamic model for cointegrated series in which short-run changes respond to lagged changes plus an error-correction term measuring the deviation from the long-run equilibrium, so the system adjusts back toward equilibrium over time. Its validity follows from the Granger representation theorem of Engle and Granger (1987).
concept.intuition: The cointegrating spread acts like a rubber band: when last period's gap from equilibrium was wide, today's changes pull the series back toward it, at a speed set by the adjustment coefficient.
concept.mechanics: Estimate the long-run cointegrating vector, form the equilibrium error z_{t-1} = y_{t-1} - beta x_{t-1}, and regress Delta y_t on lagged changes of both series plus alpha z_{t-1}; a negative, significant alpha confirms error correction. In the vector setting (VECM) each equation carries its own loading on the equilibrium errors.
concept.formula: Delta y_t = alpha (y_{t-1} - beta x_{t-1}) + sum_i gamma_i Delta y_{t-i} + sum_j delta_j Delta x_{t-j} + epsilon_t, where alpha < 0 is the speed of adjustment and (y - beta x) the equilibrium error.
concept.failure_modes: Everything hinges on the estimated cointegrating vector: if it is misspecified or unstable, the error-correction term injects noise rather than signal. Adjustment may be asymmetric or threshold-type in practice, which the linear ECM misses.
concept.misconceptions: That the error-correction term by itself shows which variable does the adjusting: the loading coefficients must be estimated (weak exogeneity tested), and interpreting alpha as causality carries the usual reduced-form cautions.
concept.example: Modeling consumption changes as Delta c_t = -0.2 (c_{t-1} - 0.9 y_{t-1}) + short-run dynamics implies consumption closes about 20% of its gap from the long-run income relationship each quarter.
